newsitem.title: USA: Developed markets see Q4 business growth -- survey.
newsitem.headline: Developed markets see Q4 business growth -- survey.

text.p: Businesses in North America, Europe and the Pacific region generally see sustained growth through the end of 1996, according to Dun & Bradstreet's fourth-quarter International Survey of Business Expectations.
This was the third consecutive quarter of optimism for steady growth in net sales and net profits, the survey said.

"At the close of the year, executives in most developed markets worldwide expect 1996 to be characterized by consistent quarter-to-quarter growth in sales and profits, moderate prices and generally high employment," said Joseph Duncan, chief economic advisor to Dun & Bradstreet Corp.
Executives in nearly every region surveyed expect their net sales and net profits to grow at levels comparable to the prior quarter, the survey said.
The World Net Sales Index was unchanged at 45 and the Net Profits Index rose two points to 35.
As in recent surveys, North America expressed the strongest optimism for growth, Duncan said.
The Net Sales Index for North America was unchanged at 52 and the Net Profits Index increased two points to 44.
Businesses in the United States and Canada predict strong, steady growth in both indexes, the survey said.
Mexico, which participated in the survey for the first time since the peso's devaluation in mid 1995, also registered very strong expectations, Duncan said.
"In every region surveyed, there are reasons to be optimistic about the world economy," Duncan said.

"With very few exceptions, the European nations surveyed look for continued strong expansion through year's end. After three years of steady growth, the United States appears to be moving toward more moderate expansion without encountering high inflation."
In the Pacific region, executives in both Australia and New Zealand expect peak sales growth for the year to take place in the fourth quarter, Duncan said.

Most nations included in the survey expected selling prices and employment levels to continue growing at about the same pace as in the third quarter, the survey said. They also predict inventories will remain near the levels forecast in the third-quarter survey.
